sections.h2: Where do I deal with property tax in Houston County, Georgia?
sections.html:
Houston County runs property tax through two separate departments, plus city offices that bill their own levies. The Tax Commissioner collects county and school taxes at two locations. The Tax Assessors, who value property and take homestead applications, work from the Perry courthouse complex. The assessors' own FAQ says the assessor's office does not handle billing at all.

Both Tax Commissioner offices keep Monday to Friday hours of 8:30 AM to 5:00 PM. The Warner Robins office is at the Carl Vinson Parkway address above. Online payment carries a convenience fee, and the county's online payment portal also lets you search taxes by parcel.

sections.h2: What should a seller know about Houston County itself?
sections.html:
Houston County was created on May 15, 1821 and named for Governor John Houstoun, with the spelling later shortened. The village of Wattsville was picked as the seat because it sat in the middle of the new county, and by 1824 the town incorporated under the name Perry, which the county's statistics page calls the geographic center of Georgia. Perry later earned the nickname Crossroads of Georgia because two national highways crossed there. By 1870 the county was known for peach orchards.

Warner Robins grew from the depot built on cotton fields near Wellston during World War II. The town incorporated on March 5, 1943. Centerville followed in 1958, named for its position between Macon and Perry. Interstate 75 came through in the 1960s, and Robins Air Force Base is now the largest employer in Houston County and the fourth largest in Georgia, according to the county history.

  • Total area: 375.54 square miles, ranked 67th of Georgia's 159 counties.
  • Road miles: 1,088.2, of which 94.5% are paved.
  • Incorporated cities: Centerville, Perry and Warner Robins.
  • Landmark: the Georgia National Fairgrounds & Agricenter, which opened in 1990.

sections.h2: What do the Census numbers say about Houston County housing?
sections.html:
The Census Bureau's July 2025 estimate is 178,214 residents, up 8.9% from the April 2020 base. Housing units totaled 74,635, and the county issued 1,218 building permits in 2025. Workers report a mean travel time of 22.8 minutes, shorter than the 34.9 minutes in Heard County or 33.1 in Henry County.

  • Median value of owner-occupied homes, 2020 to 2024: $219,800.
  • Owner-occupied rate: 66.9%, meaning about a third of households rent.
  • Median gross rent: $1,208.
  • Median household income: $80,698.
  • Bachelor's degree or higher, age 25 and up: 32.5%.

Sellers who rented a house out before listing it should check whether the homestead exemption still applies, because the county describes the exemption as applying to property the taxpayer owns and occupies as a legal residence.

sections.h2: How does Houston County value property for tax?
sections.html:
The Tax Commissioner's page explains that fair market value is set as of January 1 each year, and the tax is levied on an assessed value fixed by law at 40% of that figure. One mill equals $1.00 for each $1,000 of assessed value. The Board of Tax Assessors sends a notice whenever it changes a value from the prior year or from what the owner returned.

Real property returns on the state PT-50R form and applications for conservation use, exempt status and similar programs must be mailed with a US postmark no later than April 1. Personal property returns, due the same date, are accepted by mail only. Boat, aircraft and business owners get their forms in January. Real estate questions go to (478) 218-4750, and records are searchable at the county's qpublic site.

Because the assessors do not bill, a seller wondering whether a city levy was paid has to call Warner Robins, Perry or Centerville directly. County and school tax confirmation comes from the Tax Commissioner.

sections.h2: How do I get a homestead exemption in Houston County?
sections.html:
File the initial application with the Tax Assessor's Office by April 1 of the year you first claim it. Once granted, the exemption renews on its own each year. You apply again only if ownership changes or you want to qualify for a different exemption.

The state's standard exemption knocks $2,000 off assessed value, and many counties add local exemptions that are larger, according to the Department of Revenue. Local amounts vary by county, so ask the assessors at (478) 218-4750 what applies to your parcel. A buyer who closes mid-year should ask the assessors how the purchase date affects first-year eligibility.

sections.h2: How do I appeal a Houston County assessment?
sections.html:
You have 45 days from the date the assessment notice was mailed. File the appeal with the Board of Tax Assessors, which reviews its valuation and tells you its decision. If you are still unhappy, the appeal goes to the County Board of Equalization, where a hearing is scheduled and the board decides at the hearing's end. Superior court is the next step, and arbitration is offered in place of the Board of Equalization.

  • Grounds allowed: taxability, the value placed on the property, or uniformity compared with similar properties.
  • Grounds not allowed: a complaint about the amount of tax levied.
  • Hearing officer track: non-homestead real property above $500,000 only.
  • Arbitration track: value only, supported by a certified appraisal.

The Department of Revenue notes that after a board decision you have 30 days to give written notice of a superior court appeal, and the prior year's taxes must be paid before the court hears it. Houston County's tax commissioner page directs property tax questions to taxquestions@houstoncountyga.gov.

sections.h2: When are Houston County taxes due, and what about taxes at closing?
sections.html:
Houston's tax commissioner pages list no fixed due date, so use the date on your bill or call (478) 542-2110. Georgia's default due date is December 20, and counties may move it to December 1 or November 15 or bill in installments. The state allows 60 days from the bill's postmark before interest begins.

Ownership on January 1 decides who owes the year's tax, and Georgia law gives no refund to a seller who leaves partway through the year. When a Perry or Warner Robins house sells, ask the closing agent for the county, school and city tax lines separately, since the cities bill on their own.

A lien can be recorded when a tax bill goes unpaid, and the property can later be sold at auction. Georgia's Consumer Ed office says there is a twelve-month redemption period afterward, at the bid amount plus later taxes, special assessments and a 20% premium.

faqs.q: Does the Houston County Tax Assessor send tax bills?
faqs.a: No. The assessors' FAQ says the office does not handle billing. Use the Tax Commissioner at (478) 542-2110 in Warner Robins or (478) 218-4940 in Perry for county bills, and the cities of Warner Robins, Perry or Centerville for city levies.

faqs.q: What is the deadline to file a Houston County homestead exemption?
faqs.a: April 1 of the year you first claim the exemption. The application goes to the Tax Assessor's Office, and once approved the exemption renews automatically unless ownership changes or you apply for a different exemption.

faqs.q: How many days do I have to appeal a Houston County assessment?
faqs.a: Forty-five days from the date the assessment notice was mailed. The appeal goes to the Board of Tax Assessors first. You cannot appeal on the ground that the tax amount is too high, only on taxability, value or uniformity.

faqs.q: Where are the Houston County Tax Commissioner offices?
faqs.a: One is at 202 Carl Vinson Parkway in Warner Robins and the other is at 201 Perry Parkway in Perry. Both are open Monday to Friday from 8:30 AM to 5:00 PM.

faqs.q: Who pays Houston County property tax when a house sells mid-year?
faqs.a: The owner on January 1 owes the full year under Georgia law, with no refund for partial-year ownership. Ask the closing agent to itemize the county, school and city tax lines.
